purpose: Shared numeric digit encoding for HUD, level introduction and high scores, separated from drawing, ASCII conversion and blanking.

inputs: AL byte, AX unsigned word, or DX:AX 32-bit bit pattern becomes uint8/uint16/uint32 value
DecimalOutput: positive capacity, initialized writable bytes, cursor below capacity; 65536-byte ring is the DOS boundary
DecimalDivisors: live byte references to ten, hundred, little-endian thousand and ten-thousand words
outputs: Exactly 2/4/6 numeric bytes plus FF sentinel on success; cursor points at sentinel, not past it
DecimalResult reports division status, final packed remainder pair and thousand-stage remainder for bridge diagnostics
effects: Reads each divisor immediately before its division, after earlier ordered digit writes
Writes numeric leading zeros; never ASCII or leading-blank suppression
Retains partial output and intermediate arithmetic diagnostics on L1 unsupported-division paths
preconditions: Output metadata and the divisor-reference struct do not alias the byte storage they describe
Divisor bytes may alias output or each other; they must remain accessible and initialized for every performed read
Bridge storage is ordinary RAM with no instruction bytes, VGA, live L0 save/return stack or concurrent writers
DOS successful-return contract requires every division nonzero and quotient representable; L0 divide faults are outside it
interface.projection: Bridge borrows the actual shared RAM ring and live divisor addresses; no divisor snapshot. AX/DX diagnostic projections are retained; BX/CX and other shell values remain untouched. IF/DF are preserved, and digit cursor always increments independent of DF.
interface.errors: DECIMAL_DIVISION_ERROR maps to L1 UGH_UNSUPPORTED with partial writes; this is not an emulation or equivalence proof for L0 INT 0.
format_examples: six(1000000) begins with byte 10; six(25600000) wraps its first-byte count to zero
The six-digit loop subtracts at least once and tests the signed high word. High unsigned inputs can stop immediately or traverse the wrap boundary; no unsigned quotient rewrite is made.

callers.observations: CurrentLevelIndex increment wraps as byte, then numeric buffer at C8; caller adds 48 to tens/units for title text. ADD defines arithmetic flags before use.
Reads six C8 bytes, performs its own ASCII and leading-zero-to-space conversion. XOR/AND/CMP define flags before tests; no encoder arithmetic flag result.
C8 and CF numeric/sentinel buffers. First call must preserve CX previous score high word and BX low word; second enters comparison tail that XORs SI and CMPs bytes before branches.
C8/CF buffers; BX preserved for previous value; shared comparison tail defines tested flags.
C8/CF buffers; BL previous value retained; comparison tail defines flags. Shared four/two falls are internal, not independent contracts.

L0: Six falls through four, four falls through two; no external application callee

indirect.classification: No indirect transfer in encoder; three public entries and direct internal shared tails.

read: DS:00BD byte ten=10, 00BE byte hundred=100, 00BF word thousand=1000, 00C1 word ten-thousand=10000 in shipped DGROUP
Live reads follow earlier writes, including intentional output-over-divisor aliases
write: Borrowed DS:SI numeric bytes and sentinel, per-byte cursor wraps at FFFF
C8..CE current digits/sentinel and CF..D5 previous digits/sentinel in the HUD; menu also uses C8
owners: Decimal group interprets divisors as configuration; initial storage is DGROUP data
Borrowed digit buffers consumed by HUD/front-end; ASCII formatting and draw caches remain caller-owned
memory.aliases: Divisors are read-only in ordinary use, not assumed immutable: output aliases can modify later divisors. Word divisor bytes are contiguous, not individually cursor-wrapped.

assumptions: No whole-program score/range invariant is used to normalize out-of-range inputs
Full 65536-byte output ring for DOS bridge; smaller capacities are explicit native extensions
Known caller flag liveness is conditional on normal call/return and no code/stack corruption
